title: In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a TPU
hook: Google built a custom chip whose heart is a 256x256 grid of 8-bit multiply-accumulate units - and in production it ran neural-net inference roughly 15-30x faster than the GPUs and CPUs of its day.
key_points: The TPU is a custom ASIC for neural-network inference, deployed in Google datacenters since 2015.
Its core is a 65,536 (256x256) 8-bit multiply-accumulate matrix-multiply unit, peaking at 92 TeraOps/second.
Carries 28 MiB of on-chip memory to keep data close to the compute.
In production it ran inference about 15x-30x faster than contemporary GPUs/CPUs, at roughly 30x-80x better performance per watt.
content_html: Norman Jouppi and his coauthors at Google opened up the Tensor Processing Unit, a custom ASIC the company had quietly been running in its datacenters since 2015 to serve neural-network inference. The paper is a rare in-production look at why a purpose-built chip can leave general-purpose hardware far behind on this one job.
extra_html:
How it works

The TPU is built around a 65,536-cell (256x256) matrix-multiply unit of 8-bit multiply-accumulate (MAC) operators, giving a peak of 92 TeraOps/second. Rather than shuttle data back and forth to off-chip memory, it keeps 28 MiB of memory on the chip itself, close to the compute, which is what lets the big MAC array stay fed. Because it targets inference specifically, it can lean on low-precision integer math instead of the general-purpose floating-point machinery a CPU or GPU carries.

Why it matters

In Google's production workloads the TPU ran inference about 15x-30x faster than the contemporary GPUs and CPUs it was compared against, and roughly 30x-80x better on performance per watt - the metric that actually matters when you are filling a datacenter. The paper became a landmark argument that domain-specific silicon, not just faster general-purpose chips, would shape the economics of deploying deep learning at scale.
